entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
Read about Canadian history from 1800-1900 through books that immerse students in the time period and allow them to see the world through the eyes of those who lived it. Through engaging narratives, biographies, history spines, primary source documents, oral histories, historical fiction, and books that show different perspectives, students come to see history as more than dates and events and develop relationships with people from the past. Viewing images, looking at maps, and working on one's Book of Centuries are also part of developing this relationship.

This topic is included in the following course(s): History: Grades 7-8 (Canada)

blocks.text:
• Read through the lesson and gather any necessary links. 

• If you have not read the book, you may want to read the selected pages in advance. 

• Decide which lessons/books to read together and which to have students read independently.

• Connect back to the previous lesson. Have students give a summary of what they remember. (Full narration is not necessary.)

• If the previous passage is difficult to remember, teachers may ask a leading question: "What can you tell me about..." Or students may try looking back at any chapter/section headings or illustrations or reading the first paragraph to jog the memory.

• Use a picture, map, or engaging question to pique the student's interest in the day's lesson (often included in lesson plans). 

• If necessary, talk about a few unfamiliar words that will be crucial to understanding.

• Read the day's passage out loud or have the student read independently. Sometimes reading for the specified time is a better guide.

• If a book is challenging, try stopping to narrate every now and then rather than waiting until the end. It can also help to read aloud. Or you might want to use an audiobook version of the text and have students read along with it.

• Have students keep an eye out for events or characters to add to their Citizenship Notebook, Book of Centuries, or Copywork Book.

• Have students retell the passage orally or write a narration. 

• Alternatively, students might analyze a character, trace cause to consequence, outline a passage, or use one of the other methods indicated by Charlotte Mason in School Education Chapter 16, especially p.180.

• Students who enjoy writing can experiment with different types of written narrations, but this is not required.

• Give the student an opportunity to share thoughts on the lesson and any connections made (orally or in writing). 

• You could ask them what they thought about the passage or ask an open-ended question to stimulate discussion. Discussion questions are often included in the lesson plans.
• Optional: Add something to the Book of Centuries, Century Chart, Citizenship Notebook, or Commonplace book. If students would like to include pictures, these may be drawn or printed.

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 1
lessons.body:
Introduction - The War of 1812
⍞ Materials: Jeremy's War 1812

➜ INTRO
Throughout much of the eighteenth century and into the second decade of the nineteenth century, the British Navy was engaged in near-continuous naval conflicts until peace was declared in 1815, after the Battle of Waterloo. One of Britain's last major battles before then was the War of 1812, in which Canada, then still a collection of British colonies, became the battleground for a conflict between the United States and Britain over many long-standing grievances, including shipping rights and American expansionist plans. 
The first historical novel we will read in this course is Jeremy's War 1812, a gripping account of the war told from the perspective of a fifteen-year-old orphaned boy who joins a regiment of British soldiers and eventually becomes the personal servant of Sir Isaac Brock. Historical details blend smoothly with a fictional story to create a detailed recreation of this definitive period in Canada's pre-Confederation history.

➜ VIEW
The following video gives some background on the stakes for Canada in the War of 1812 and its importance for Canada's history.
∞ Video Link: The War of 1812 | The Canadian Perspective 

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.7-18 "They were expecting me" - "and walked inside."

• Who are the characters you meet as the novel opens? How are they related to each other? What are they like? You may choose to keep a character list with some notes.

The War of 1812, cont.
⍞ Materials: Jeremy's War 1812

➜ RECAP

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.33-46 "It was hard to sleep" - "have General Brock."

• Explain the causes of the War of 1812 as they are presented in today's reading. What makes Captain Stanton hopeful for success?

➜ VIEW
Take a few minutes to look at this map of York, now Toronto, made in 1813. In today's reading, Jeremy travels south on Yonge St. (most likely the sole road on this map that stretches north through the forest). Notice in the "Remark" on the map, that bridges over the Don River to the east of York were "decaying fast" and "in so great danger of falling that it was thought requisite at this time (Nov. 1813) to support." While the bridge that collapsed under Jeremy was north rather than east of York, this map shows that at this time, bridges could be hazardous for travellers.
∞ Map Link: 1813 Sketch of York

lessons.body:
The War of 1812
⍞ Materials: The Story of Canada

➜ INTRO
Now that we've learned the fate of General Brock, we will pause from reading Jeremy's War for a lesson and read a historical overview of the War of 1812. If you have any extra time at the end of the lesson, you can continue to explore the 1812 Virtual Exhibition.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS

p.92 and 94 (skip page 93) "A few years later" - "into the North."

➜ VIEW
1\. Spend some time looking at this engraving of The Battle of Queenston Heights. The original engraving this one is based on is attributed to Captain James Dennis, who fought in the battle. The Americans (in blue) are crossing the Niagara River to Queenston (the right side) from Lewiston (the left side).
∞ Image Link: The Battle of Queenston Heights

2\. Visit Brock's Monument at Queenston Heights. You don't need to watch the whole video, but the drone footage provides an amazing view!
∞ Video Link: Canada's Most Imposing War Memorial

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 17
lessons.body:
The Métis & The Red River Settlement
⍞ Materials: The Story of Canada; map or atlas of Canada that includes Manitoba

➜ INTRO
While the War of 1812 was at its height in Upper and Lower Canada to the east, a Scottish nobleman named Thomas Douglas, 5th Earl of Selkirk, was working to establish a colony on the prairies to the west, at the intersection of the Red and Assiniboine Rivers, near what is now Winnipeg. Selkirk had received a large grant of land from the Hudson Bay Company and wanted to create a farming community to support many poor Scottish Highlanders and Irish peasants, who had lost their homes and livelihoods due to various upheavals at the end of the eighteenth century. This community, known as the Red River Settlement, would come to play a large role in the history of immigrants to the prairies, the Métis peoples, the province of Manitoba, and the history of Canada as a nation.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.114-120 "In April 1806" - "cries of despair."

➜ MAPPING ACTIVITY
Look at a map or atlas of Manitoba (online is fine) and locate the Red River and Fort Douglas (present-day Winnipeg). Find the Hudson Bay on the same map so you can see the route the settlers took.
Compare this modern map to a map of the land given to Selkirk:
∞ Map Link: Map showing the Selkirk Land Grant in 1811

➜ VIEW
Learn more about elements of Métis culture, several of which are mentioned in today's reading: Métis sash, Red River cart, Red River jig, Métis flag, cuisine, beadwork, and fiddle. Follow the "Learn More" links under each heading.
∞ Link: Symbols of Métis Culture

Rebellion and Reform
⍞ Materials: The Story of Canada

➜ RECAP
What did you read about immigration to Canada in the early nineteenth century?

➜ INTRO
How do we choose our government in Canada and in our provinces and territories? Do you think it has always been this way in Canada? Today, we will learn about frustrations towards the government in the 1830s, which would eventually lead to the form of government we recognize today.

➜ VIEW
Remember that in 1791, the large Province of Quebec was divided into Upper and Lower Canada, roughly corresponding to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec today.
∞ Link: Upper & Lower Canada in 1791

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.93 "Bytown and Ottawa"
p.94-97 "In the 1830s" - "disguised in women's clothing"

• What changes did William Lyon Mackenzie want to see in Upper Canada?

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 20
lessons.body:
Sophie's Rebellion
⍞ Materials: Sophie's Rebellion

➜ RECAP
What do you remember from the last reading about the discontent and rebellions in Lower Canada (now Quebec)?

➜ INTRO
Sophie's Rebellion is a fictional account of one American girl's experience of the 1837-1838 Rebellions, as she is caught up in the Battle of Beauharnois. Through Sophie's eyes, the reader is able to see multiple perspectives of this conflict and is introduced to a number of notable historical figures. The novel also provides an authentically detailed account of Upper and Lower Canada in the mid-nineteenth century.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.7-23 "The Rebellion of 1838" - "to have them."

• The book opens with a mysterious character named Luc. What do you know about him, and what questions do you still have?
• Who are the characters you meet as the novel opens? How are they related to each other? What are they like? What historical events have they been involved in, and where do their loyalties lie? You may choose to keep a character list with some notes.

➜ VIEW
Look at the map below to see just how close Burlington, VT and Lake Champlain are to the Canadian border and Montreal.
∞ Map Link: Vermont & Quebec Map
lessons.teacherNotes:
• EXTRA HELPING
Students who would like extra background on the Patriote Rebellion against Lower Canada Loyalists are encouraged to watch this video. While the narration is in French, the auto-translated English subtitles are very accurate.
∞ Video Link: Patriot Rebellions in Quebec (1837-1838)

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 39
lessons.body:
Pre-Confederation Years
⍞ Materials: The Charlottetown Conference

➜ INTRO
You may have heard of Canada's "Fathers of Confederation" and that Charlottetown, PEI, is sometimes called the "Birthplace of Confederation," but what really happened in the 1860s that led to Canada becoming a country? The next book we will read, The Charlottetown Conference and the Birth of Confederation, is a detailed account of the historical factors, issues, political players, and conferences that eventually led to Canada's Confederation in 1867. The book brings this historical period to life with numerous photographs, paintings, archival documents, and other primary sources, so be sure to spend some of your lesson time looking at the photos.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.1-8 "Robert Harris was several" - "wait another eight years."

➜ NOTEBOOK
This book gives you an excellent chance to practice note-taking and finding information for a Century Chart or Book of Centuries. Look for important figures and significant dates and add them to a note-keeping format of your own choosing.

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 40
lessons.body:
Elijah of Buxton
⍞ Materials: Elijah of Buxton

➜ INTRO
The third historical fiction novel we will read this year is the story of eleven-year old Elijah, the first child born free in the town of Buxton, Ontario, a settlement of runaway slaves and free Black people that was a haven of safety and hope, especially in the years leading up to the Civil War. 

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
1\. p.343-345 Read the Author's Note to get an introduction to the town of Buxton and the historical context for the novel.
2\. p.1-17 "It was Sunday after church" - "lets you know you're wrong."

• Start a character chart and write short descriptions of the people mentioned. You will continue to add to this chart as you read through the novel.
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
The novel is written from Elijah's first-person perspective, in his own distinct colloquial dialect. The audiobook version, with excellent narration by Mirron Willis, is a good option for getting a sense of the patterns of Elijah's language.

terms.content:
· Jeremy's War: Explain who Tecumseh was and his role in the War of 1812. OR Describe the events leading up to and the outcome of the Siege of Detroit, with particular attention to General Brock's decisions.

· The Story of Canada: Describe Métis culture in the West: who are they, how did they live, and what was life like for them in the first decades of the nineteenth century? OR Explain why there was discontent in Upper and Lower Canada towards the government.

· Sophie's Rebellion: The novel features French Canadian, British, American, and English Canadian characters. Describe the attitudes and interactions of some of these groups towards each other, as depicted in the novel. OR Write a letter from Sophie to her father, describing all that happened in Beauharnois.

· The Story of Canada and The Charlottetown Conference: Describe what life was like in Canada in the mid-nineteenth century, in the years leading up to Confederation. OR Explain how responsible government works.

· The Charlottetown Conference: Describe how the Charlottetown Conference and the meetings that came after led to the founding of Canada in 1867. OR Choose one prominent figure you learned about who attended the Charlottetown Conference, and explain why their contribution to Canada's history was important.

· Elijah of Buxton: Describe the history of Buxton, including how it came to be, who lived there, what their homes, school, and other buildings were like, and why Buxton is important to learn about in Canadian History. OR Explain how Elijah changes from the beginning of the novel to the end. Why is he called "fra-gile" at first, and how does he eventually become the hero of the story?
